summary: Extends PPPoE with a credit-based flow control mechanism and a link quality metric report. It is meant to improve performance over media such as mobile radio with variable bandwidth and limited buffering. It is informational and was replaced by RFC 5578.

plainLanguage.summary: Over a bumpy wireless link, a sender should only send what the receiver has room for. This adds a way to give out space credits and report link quality.

subtitle: Credit-based flow control and link metrics for PPP over Ethernet.

tldr.problem: PPP over Ethernet works well when both endpoints have similar and stable bandwidth, but fails on links with variable bandwidth and limited buffering, like mobile radio. The sender can overwhelm the receiver.
tldr.mechanism: This extension adds credit-based flow control to PPPoE discovery and session stages, and introduces a link quality metrics report. Senders grant credits (buffers) to receivers before sending, and both sides report link quality metrics such as data rate, latency, and signal quality.
tldr.outcome: Deployments with variable-bandwidth links can manage buffering better and make routing decisions based on link quality. The standard remains specialized for wireless and similar scenarios.

facts.label: Link metrics reported
facts.value: Data rate (kbps), latency (ms), RLQ, resources, receive-only flag

today: RFC 4938 is Informational and describes an extension to PPPoE for specialized radio and satellite deployments. It was superseded by RFC 5578, though the underlying principle of credit-based flow control remains relevant to systems with limited buffering and variable bandwidth.

sections.title: The Problem and the Solution
sections.content:
PPP over Ethernet (PPPoE) encapsulates PPP sessions over Ethernet, allowing hosts and access concentrators to negotiate and maintain protocol connections. It works well when both endpoints have similar, stable bandwidth. However, many deployments involve variable bandwidth and limited buffering, such as radio links. When a faster access concentrator sends to a slower radio receiver with small buffers, the receiver's buffers fill and packets are discarded. The sender has no feedback about available buffer space.

This RFC extends PPPoE with credit-based flow control and link quality metrics. In the credit model, a sender can only transmit after the receiver grants it credits (measured in 64-byte units). Credits represent buffer availability. The receiver reports link metrics such as current and maximum data rates, latency, relative link quality (RLQ), and remaining resources (like battery power). This allows both in-band and out-of-band credit management during the PPPoE session.
sections.plainLanguage: A radio link is like a narrow pipe connected to a small bucket. PPPoE flow control is the sender asking, "How much can I send?" and waiting for the receiver to say, "I have room for 5 buckets," before sending.

sections.title: Discovery Stage Extensions
sections.content:
PPPoE has two stages: Discovery (where the client finds the server and negotiates parameters) and Session (where PPP frames are exchanged). This RFC extends the Discovery stage with new packet types and optional tags. During discovery, the host may request credit flow control by including a Credit Tag in the PADR (PPPoE Active Discovery Request). The tag contains two fields: FCN (Forward Credit Notification, credits the host grants to the access concentrator) and BCN (Backward Credit Notification, initially zero).

If the access concentrator supports credit flow, it echoes the Credit Tag in its PADS (session confirmation) response, setting its own FCN (credits granted to the host) and echoing the host's FCN as its BCN. This exchange signals that both sides agree to credit-based operation for the entire session. Additionally, this RFC introduces the PADG (Active Discovery Session-Grant) and PADC (Active Discovery Session-Credit Response) packets, used to grant incremental credits out-of-band, and the PADQ (Active Discovery Quality) packet, which reports or queries link metrics.
sections.plainLanguage: When the radio and access concentrator first meet, they agree: "I'll let you send 100 units before you need to ask again." This happens before any data flows.

sections.title: Credit Flow Control Mechanism
sections.content:
Credits represent buffer space, measured in 64-byte units. One unit of credit is 64 bytes, so a grant of 4 credits equals 256 bytes. The credit model distinguishes out-of-band credits (exchanged in PADG/PADC packets during discovery and mid-session) and in-band credits (piggybacked on PPP Session stage packets). Once a credit-based session is established, a sender maintains a running credit counter. With each transmitted packet, the counter decrements. When it reaches zero, the sender stops transmitting until the receiver grants more credits via a PADG packet.

The receiver maintains its own counter of credits it has granted. When it receives a PADG, it adds the incremental credits to its counter. The receiver responds with a PADC packet echoing the new absolute credit count. Both sides track both their granted credits and received credits. If there are transmission errors, the BCN (Backward Credit Notification) field helps nodes resynchronize their credit counts. The maximum outstanding credit is 0xffff (65535), representing about 4 megabytes of buffer.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender keeps a note of how many "passes" it has to send. Each message uses one pass. When it runs out, it stops and waits for the receiver to give it more passes.

sections.title: Link Quality Metrics and Reporting
sections.content:
The PADQ packet carries link quality information in a Metric Tag, which includes six fields. Receive-only flag indicates whether the link is bidirectional or receive-only. Maximum data rate and current data rate are reported in kilobits per second (kbps). Latency is the transmission delay in milliseconds. Resources is a percentage (0-100) indicating available resources such as battery power. Relative Link Quality (RLQ) is a non-dimensional score from 0 (poorest) to 100 (best).

The PADQ can be used in two modes: a query (metric tag length zero) or a report (metric tag with values). Either endpoint can autonomously send PADQ reports to advertise changing link conditions. For example, when signal quality degrades or available bandwidth drops, the radio can send a PADQ report so the access concentrator can make better routing decisions or adjust expectations. Nodes may throttle the rate of autonomous PADQ packets to avoid overwhelming the peer. PADQ queries are retransmitted with exponential backoff if no response is received.
sections.plainLanguage: The radio can tell the access concentrator: "My signal is good, I can send data at 1 Mbps, but my battery is at 20%." This helps the router decide where to send traffic.

sections.title: Session Stage and Operational Status
sections.content:
During the PPP Session stage, credit tags can be piggybacked on data packets for in-band flow control. When the parser detects that the field immediately after the PPP Session LENGTH is not the standard PPP protocol identifier (0xc021), it treats the field as a TLV (Type-Length-Value) tag. The Credit Tag is the only optional TLV permitted in the PPP Session stage. This allows senders to grant incremental credits with each data packet, which is efficient during high-traffic periods.

RFC 4722 is an Informational document addressing a specific deployment scenario: radio systems with split PPP and radio termination separated by Ethernet. The IETF PPPEXT working group noted in the IESG note that solving flow control at the PPP layer may have unpredictable interactions with higher protocols, and recommends avoiding split termination in favor of standard routing. Nevertheless, RFC 5578 later updated this specification. The technique remains useful in specialized wireless and satellite deployments.
sections.plainLanguage: While the data is flowing, small credit updates can ride along on each message. After standardization, better approaches emerged, but this method works for radio systems.
